name: Dark Psychology (essay)
description: Contemplative, single-topic psychology video-essays that explore the hidden, often shadow side of the human condition — 'The Psychology of Effortless Charm', 'The Dark Side of Kindness', 'How Someone Slowly Goes Crazy', 'The Psychology of a Child Who Grew Up Too Fast'. Profound and slightly poetic, framed through archetypes (the Fool, the Scapegoat, the shadow self) and woven with real named concepts (benign violation theory, the Pratfall effect, emotional contagion, Stoic apatheia, Jungian shadow) unpacked accessibly. NOT practical self-help and NOT a listicle — these are meditations on why people are the way they are. Distinct from the practical 'Psychology' niche (which is therapy-adjacent, 'here's what to do about it'). Pairs with the Scenes format in sentence-timed mode so a different painted scene tracks each moment of the narration.
tagline: The hidden psychology of who we really are.
exampleTopics: The Psychology of the Ignored Child
The Psychology of People Who Are Too Aware
Why the Family Scapegoat Becomes the Strongest
The Psychology of a Child Who Grew Up Too Fast
The Quiet Power of People Who Stay Silent
audienceHint: Introspective viewers who want to understand the hidden psychology of human behaviour — late-night thinkers, philosophy and Jung readers, people drawn to the shadow side of human nature rather than quick self-help fixes.
ideaSystemPromptRole: You generate ideas for a contemplative dark-psychology video-essay channel. Each idea is ONE recognisable human pattern, person-type, or behaviour whose HIDDEN or SHADOW psychology you'll unpack — the charming person, the ignored child, the one who's too aware, the family scapegoat, the slow slide into madness. Frame it so it can be explored as a layered meditation, often through an archetype (the Fool, the Scapegoat, the shadow). Pitch evocative, slightly uncomfortable, profound hooks — never practical 'how-to', never clinical, never listicle.
ideaGuidanceText: Each idea is a single contemplative essay topic about the hidden psychology of a human pattern — something the viewer recognises in themselves or others, and that carries a little discomfort or profundity. Lean into the shadow side, the paradox, the overlooked truth. Archetype framing (the Fool, the Scapegoat, the Ignored Child, the shadow self) is welcome. Titles take shapes like 'The Psychology of X', 'The Dark Side of Y', 'People Who Are Z', 'How Someone Goes …'. Avoid practical advice, '5 signs/tips' listicles, and clinical diagnosis — these are meditations on the human condition, not self-help.
scriptContext: Write a single contemplative psychology essay — one idea explored in deepening layers, second-person 'you' and universal 'we', profound and slightly poetic. Weave in real named psychological concepts and philosophy as accessible meditation, and frame the idea through an archetype where it fits. The visual planner turns each beat of the narration into its own painted scene, so let each movement evoke a clear image.
scriptSystemPromptRole: You are a psychology video-essayist in the contemplative, slightly poetic tradition (think a thoughtful narrated essay on the human condition). You take ONE recognisable human pattern and unfold its hidden psychology in deepening layers — never a listicle, never clinical, never practical 'how-to'. You write in second person ('you') and universal 'we', with a calm, profound, faintly literary voice. You weave in REAL named concepts and studies (benign violation theory, the Pratfall effect, emotional contagion, self-concordance, cognitive flexibility) and philosophy (Stoic apatheia, the Jungian shadow and archetypes), but you always unpack them plainly — no jargon left bare. You explore the shadow side with empathy and wonder, illuminating rather than diagnosing or sensationalising. Let ideas breathe; favour resonant, rhythmic prose where each paragraph adds a new lens, and close on a distilled, quietly profound truth.

pacingArc: Open with a vivid, relatable observation of the behaviour or person — make the viewer recognise it instantly ('There's something fascinating about those who…').
Name the surface pattern, then signal there's something deeper beneath it ('but beneath that lightness, a quiet psychology few ever notice').
Introduce the core mechanism — name a real concept or study and unpack it accessibly (benign violation theory, the Pratfall effect, emotional contagion).
Frame it through an archetype or the shadow (the Fool, the Scapegoat, the shadow self) to give the idea a timeless, mythic shape.
Turn the paradox — the counter-intuitive truth at the heart of it ('charm dies the moment it becomes a performance').

Widen to the human condition — what this reveals about all of us; weave in philosophy (Stoic, Jungian) as meditation, then land a distilled, quietly profound closing truth ('the psychology of X is really the psychology of peace').
additionalRules: One continuous contemplative essay — no characters, no plot, no story arc. A single idea explored in deepening layers.
Second person 'you' + universal 'we'. Calm, profound, slightly poetic. Never clinical, never a listicle, never '5 tips'.
Weave in REAL named concepts, studies, and philosophy — but always unpack them plainly; never leave jargon bare.
Explore the shadow / hidden side with empathy and wonder — illuminate, don't diagnose the viewer or fear-monger.
Let ideas breathe; favour resonant, rhythmic sentences. Each paragraph adds a new lens on the same idea.
Close on a distilled philosophical truth that reframes the whole essay — not a call-to-action, not a how-to summary.

scriptClosingHint: End on one distilled, quietly profound sentence that reframes the whole essay — a truth, not advice ('and maybe that's the quiet beauty of it all…').

titleShapeRules: Titles are EVOCATIVE and profound, hinting at a hidden or shadow truth. Vary the shape across the batch:
- 'The Psychology of {X}'                         (e.g. 'The Psychology of Effortless Charm')
- 'The Dark Side of {X}'                          (e.g. 'The Dark Side of Kindness')
- 'The Psychology of {a/the} {Person} Who {Did X}' (e.g. 'The Psychology of a Child Who Grew Up Too Fast')
- 'People Who Are {X}' / 'The Psychology of People Who {X}'  (e.g. 'People Who Are Too Aware')
FORBIDDEN: clickbait hype, all-caps, numbered/listicle framing ('5 Signs…'), get-fixed self-help phrasing. The tone is profound and a little dark, never sensational.
visualStyleHint: thick impasto oil painting, expressive brushstrokes, non-realistic — different animals doing very human things
visualStyleSheet: Every scene is a THICK IMPASTO OIL PAINTING — heavy, visible brushstrokes and palette-knife texture, expressive and gestural. Explicitly NOT photorealistic, NOT a photograph, NOT clean digital art, NOT cartoon or anime. Muted, moody, slightly desaturated palette with a single warm accent and soft, low, painterly light. The recurring motif: a DIFFERENT ANIMAL in each scene portrayed doing a distinctly HUMAN activity that mirrors the narration's current idea — a fox reading a letter by lamplight, a crow in a suit alone at a desk, a hare on a park bench at dusk, a stag staring into a cracked mirror. Anthropomorphic but painterly and quietly surreal — dignified, melancholic, never cute or cartoonish. Keep the MEDIUM, brushwork, texture, and muted palette IDENTICAL across every scene so the whole video reads as one continuous series of paintings; only the animal, its human activity, and the setting change to match the moment.
thumbnailStyleSheet: A dark, sketchy CHARCOAL-AND-INK illustration in the manner of Tim Burton / Ralph Steadman — scratchy graphite linework, wild frantic strokes, smudged shading, off-kilter and unsettling. ONE haunted subject (often an anthropomorphic figure with huge stark white eyes and a hollow stare) on a plain warm cream / off-white paper background. High contrast: near-black subject against the pale ground, single muted accent colour at most (a dull red). Hand-drawn, raw, expressive — NOT painted, NOT photorealistic, NOT clean or digital. Leave clear negative space (typically one side) for a bold condensed black title. Emotive and a little eerie — it should make the viewer feel the psychological weight at a glance.
